content.title: Why are we going back to the moon?
content.text: The Artemis II mission heralds a new era of exploration as Nasa eyes lunar bases, rare minerals and the ultimate goal of reaching Mars The fantastic four: Jeremy Hansen, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Christina KochChip Somodevilla/GETTY IMAGES Wednesday April 01 2026, 9.00pm BST, The Times Why are humans returning to the moon 53 years after our last visit? No one at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where a cast of thousands has been preparing this week to blast four astronauts towards the moon aboard Artemis II, is in any doubt about the value of returning. The astronauts walked out in their orange space suits at 7pm UK time on Wednesday to board a van to take them to the launchpad, where their giant Space Launch System rocket had slowly and successfully been pumped full of fuel over the course of the day. The astronauts have spoken about the age-old desire to push back the frontiers of human exploration and of its importance in inspiring the next generation of scientists. Sign up for The Times’s weekly US newsletter Geologists point to the potential wealth of ice and minerals in the lunar soil. Nasa sees it as a stepping stone towards humanity’s inhabitation of worlds beyond Earth, with Mars the ultimate goal. Plus, they desperately want to achieve all this before China, which is targeting a moon landing by 2030. Nasa set out a $20 billion vision last week to build a lunar base that would make the moon become like Antarctica or the International Space Station (ISS): a remote outpost in an inhospitable location where hardy researchers live and work in shifts to carry out cutting-edge science. As Jared Isaacman, Nasa’s administrator, said, we are going back “to stay”. Artemis II launch — follow live Pioneers “Imagine if Christopher Columbus had come back from the New World, and no one returned in his footsteps.” These words are sometimes attributed to Jim Lovell, commander of Apollo 13, but were actually spoken by Tom Hanks who played Lovell in the film adaptation of that near-fatal mission. This was Hollywood poetic licence in addressing the question, which was already being raised in 1970, of why humans should return to the moon after Neil Armstrong and Apollo 11 had achieved John F Kennedy’s aim of beating the Soviet Union there in 1969. The question is being asked again as Artemis II launches three Americans and one Canadian on a “slingshot” trajectory around the moon to test the Orion spacecraft before a crewed landing. It is the first time since Apollo 17 in December 1972 that humans have left low-Earth orbit. Astronauts today mostly make the 250-mile commute to the ISS, barely skirting above our atmosphere. Now they will travel 1,000 times farther, voyaging deeper into space beyond the far side of the moon than anyone before. That extra distance will give the crew an unprecedented view. Reid Wiseman, the commander, noted from within quarantine on Sunday that 60 per cent of the moon’s far side, which faces permanently away from Earth, has never before been looked upon directly by human eyes. “The astronauts will use their geology training to photograph and interpret the lunar surface in real time,” said Megan Argo, an astrophysicist at the University of Lancashire. “This data will support future exploration and potential bases on the moon, and inform planning for longer missions, such as to Mars.” Artemis IV, scheduled for 2028, will land astronauts in the shadowy region at the moon’s southernmost point, more than 1,000 miles from the nearest Apollo landing site. Just 117 years after humans first reached the Earth’s South Pole, they aim to do the same on the moon. Aboard Artemis II, Christina Koch will be the first woman, Victor Glover the first person of colour, and Jeremy Hansen the first non-American to venture into deep space. How astronauts will spend final hours before going to the moon What more is there to learn? More than 2,500 scientific studies have been published using Apollo’s data and samples, teaching us what the moon is made of and how it once formed part of the Earth, thus revealing more about our own planet’s history. The satellite technology we rely on today was made possible through the 1960s space race. Nasa missions drove the early development of cordless power tools, memory foam, microchips and CAT scanning. Scientists from Jim al-Khalili and Brian Cox to Dame Maggie Aderin say that Apollo inspired them to go into science. If there is such value in going to the moon, why did we stay away for so long? The Apollo 17 commander, Eugene Cernan, was the last man to walk on the Moon, which he did on December 12, 1972NASA/DONALDSON COLLECTION/GETTY IMAGES “Returning to the moon has been held back by cost and lack of political or commercial incentive,” Argo said. “Since the 1970s, lunar missions have not been economically viable. That is changing. Now, there is growing global interest, China plans crewed missions within the next decade, and countries including India and Russia are discussing future landings.” Artemis II’s main mission: how to keep humans alive in space There is “a race to dominate lunar resources and key lunar sites”, said Joanne Wheeler, a space law expert at Alden. In his first term, President Trump set Nasa the goal of returning to the moon. The agency aims to do so before the end of his second term, with $93 billion dedicated so far. Lord Rees of Ludlow, the former astronomer royal, noted: “The 2020s have seen a revival of the Apollo spirit.” A trip to the lunar south pole could find ice in its shadowy craters plus oxygen-rich minerals. Lunar astronauts could source their own drinking water and breathable air and even make rocket fuel. It could also “tell us more about the history of the solar system and even how water arrived on Earth”, Argo said, filling in “gaps in our understanding” about the moon. Millions of people huddled in awe around TV screens to watch the Apollo landings in the 1960s. Artemis could see billions do the same if, as a positive contrast to war and strife on Earth, a return to the moon can capture the public imagination in anything like the same way.
